question: Which statement accurately describes memory allocation for a static member variable in Java?

options.text: A new copy is created and stored within every newly instantiated object of the class.
Memory is reallocated and wiped clean each time a static method finishes execution.
One copy is allocated when the class is loaded, and that copy is shared across all instances.
Memory is only allocated after at least one instance of the enclosing class has been created.

explanation: A static field belongs to the class itself rather than any individual object. Memory is allocated once when the class is loaded by the JVM and shared by all instances. The belief that each object gets its own copy confuses static fields with instance fields.

question: How can a public static method be invoked from an external class without creating an object?

options.text: By qualifying the method name directly with the enclosing class name, such as Math.sqrt(9.0).
By passing an implicit this reference from the caller method frame.
By creating a dummy instance with new and assigning it to an Object variable first.
By using the super keyword followed by the target method name inside any global scope.

explanation: Static methods belong to the class namespace and can be invoked directly through the class name without creating any instances. The claim that an instance must exist is incorrect because static members exist independently of object lifecycles.

question: What happens if a static method attempts to use the this keyword directly?

options.text: The compiler issues an error because this is not available in a static context.
It creates a new default instance of the class in the local stack frame.
It accesses the fields of whichever object last called that static method.
It targets the specific instance copy that was cloned when the method started.

explanation: Static methods execute without an implicit instance receiver, so the this keyword does not exist in a static context. Attempting to use this causes a compile-time error. The belief that static methods have an implicit this reference is incorrect.

question: When are static fields of a class initialized during Java program execution?

options.text: They remain uninitialized in memory until explicitly passed as an argument to new.
They are initialized when the class is first loaded, and retain their values across instantiations.
They are allocated and initialized on the execution stack each time a method exits.
They are reinitialized to their default values each time a new instance is constructed.

explanation: Static fields are initialized once when the class is loaded into the JVM. They are not reinitialized when constructors run. The misconception that creating an instance resets static variables contradicts the persistence of class-level state.
